What the frequency is telling you

The grid runs at 50 Hz, and the frequency is a direct physical readout of whether generation and demand are matching right now. More generation than demand and it rises; more demand than generation and it falls. It is not a measurement anybody takes and publishes on a schedule — it is what the spinning machinery is actually doing, sampled every 15 seconds.

⚠ Small deviations are normal and constant. The system is never exactly balanced; it is continuously pulled back towards 50 Hz by the balancing mechanism. What matters is not whether it moves but how far and for how long, which is what the panel above measures against the two limits that actually mean something.

Three readings of one thing, and none of them causes the others

Indicated imbalance, net imbalance volume and frequency all describe whether GB is short of generation or has a surplus. They are not cause and effect. One is NESO’s forecast in megawatts, one is a settled volume in megawatt-hours for a period that has closed, and one is a physical reading taken every quarter of a minute.

They will often point the same way, and when they do not, the usual reason is that they describe different windows rather than that one of them is wrong. The imbalance does not set the frequency — it is one input among many, continuously acted on, which is the whole purpose of the balancing mechanism.

Two prices, two questions

The market price is what electricity traded for on the exchanges, volume-weighted across them. The imbalance price is what parties pay for being out of balance — for using more or less than they contracted for. They answer different questions and they routinely differ by a lot.

Negative imbalance prices are ordinary on windy nights, and they are not an error: they mean the system was long and it was worth paying people to take electricity away.
